govdocs-archive_org-nsia-McRaeRobertMJud:
Charles R. Babcock reported for the Washington Post on September 14, 1978, that Memphis had agreed to stop police spying on political groups. The settlement was approved by United States District Judge Robert M. McRae Jr. It bound the city as a court order, not a promise.

Memphis police had kept political surveillance files for years, a practice exposed after the King assassination era. Suits against such spying were brought in several American cities in the 1970s. The article records the terms Memphis accepted and the judge who approved them. For the city's activists, the settlement was a legal end to being watched for their politics.
podcast-dannyjones-MH7GGdAbfjU:
Members of the Deck Hands crew join Danny Jones for KONCRETE number 9. The guest billed as Space leads a loud, loose session. The tape opens with cheers, jokes, and a lit joint.

Deck Hands grew from boat work and wild online clips. The crew trades insults, thanks, and stories with no clear plan. Jones mostly tries to keep the chaos on track. The episode is pure hangout tape: salty, silly, and proud of it. Fans of the crew will enjoy the mess; others get a taste of early Florida podcast culture.
podcast-dannyjones-mE27O8SumJU:
Author Lawrence Wright joins Danny Jones to talk about cults, dark rites, Scientology, and Israel and Palestine. Wright is a Pulitzer-winning writer known for books on faith and power. The episode title bills him as a cult investigator.

Wright shares what years of reporting taught him about groups that grip their members' lives. He moves from his Scientology work to the holy land and its long war. Jones asks how a writer earns trust in closed worlds. Listeners get the calm voice of a man who has sat with true believers of all kinds. The library files the talk as an archive record.
